John Tyler. The first vice president to assume the presidency after a sitting president's death, establishing a constitutional precedent that would guide succession for over a century. When William Henry Harrison died in 1841, Tyler asserted his right to the full presidency rather than merely acting as a caretaker, an act that redefined executive power. Though a political outsider despised by his own party, his administration oversaw territorial expansion and modernized the Office of the President.

Born in Virginia in 1790, Tyler served in Congress and as a U.S. Senator before becoming vice president in 1841. When he became president upon Harrison's death just thirty-one days into his term, he claimed the office was constitutionally his, not a temporary acting role. This assertion set a precedent that would shape all future presidential successions. Expelled from the Whig Party after refusing to adopt their economic agenda, he became a president without a party. His administration oversaw the annexation of Texas in 1845, a pivotal act that intensified sectional tensions over slavery's expansion. He strengthened presidential authority by asserting executive prerogatives against congressional demands, in effect expanding the scope and power of the modern presidency. After his term, he retired to Virginia but later returned to politics as a pro-secession Confederate congressman. His presidency illuminated enduring tensions within the federal system between executive power and congressional authority.
